How Supply Chain Leaders Can Separate Real AI Planning From the Hype

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gartner’s 2026 Hype Cycle for Agentic AI places AI agents at the Peak of Inflated Expectations.
  • Nearly every planning vendor now calls its product AI-powered, and many of the demos look alike: a chat window, a question about inventory, a quick answer.
  • Take a common scenario: a shipment delay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gartner’s 2026 Hype Cycle for Agentic AI places AI agents at the Peak of Inflated Expectations. Yet, the firm also predicted more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. Put together, those two findings describe a market where buyers are under pressure to adopt agents before they can tell which ones will hold up.

Nearly every planning vendor now calls its product AI-powered, and many of the demos look alike: a chat window, a question about inventory, a quick answer. A planner executive evaluating platforms has to work out which products will truly unlock latest capability and which just put a flashy chatbot on top of a legacy SaaS.

Take a common scenario: a shipment delay. In a traditional platform, a planner finds out about the delay via an exception report. They export data, enhancement formulas, rebuild the affected scenarios and present their recommendation in a cross-functional meeting. An AI assistant layered onto that process can proactively summarize the delay. The planner still has to rebuild the initiative by hand to see what that suggestion does to other customers, material orders and warehouses.

Agents change the planning process by working from a shared, verifiable model of the business: supplier lead times, inventory targets, production constraints and allocation rules. When the delay comes in, an agent can immediately recalculate the proposal, flags which SKUs and customers are now at risk, generates alternatives and shows the downstream effect of each one. The planner’s work moves from assembling analysis to choosing between options. This enables a real transition from reactive to proactive planning.

This gap shows up fastest under pressure. Tesla faced a cash crunch with 400,000 pre-orders to deliver during the 2018 Model 3 production ramp, and planning had to change faster than the manufacturer’s spreadsheets could keep up. The planning team built a 50-person planning engineering organization and its own software to connect sales and operations planning with day-to-day supply decisions, so a change in one part of the plan flowed through everything it touched. Over the ramp, the team cut finished-goods inventory from 75 days to 15. Few companies can justify building a planning engineering team of that size. Well-built AI planning tools can give a lean planning team that same ability to replan the whole network when something shifts.

According to recent reports, A simple test for any vendor: when a planner asks why the system recommended a change, can it show the demand assumptions, incoming shipments and inventory calculations behind it? And can it show what else in the plan moves if the planner accepts the recommendation?

According to recent reports, most of that hesitation comes down to a few practical problems. Planning data is scattered. Demand forecasts sit in one system, purchase orders in another, and supplier commitments often live in email threads and shared drives. An AI agent can only reason about the constraints it can see, so a tool connected to a partial picture will produce confident recommendations that miss the binding constraint.

Much of the most key knowledge was never written down. Experienced planners know which suppliers run late in Q4, which customers get priority when inventory is tight, and which minimum order quantities can actually be negotiated. Until those rules are captured in the planning model, AI has nothing to work from but historical data.

Many teams also hand workflows to unsupervised agents too early. Edge cases that an experienced planner handles by instinct will break an agent that was never told about them. The projects that stick start with the planner who already does the work. That person defines the workflow, monitors the agent and approves what it produces at set checkpoints. Once planners build a daily habit with the tool, it stays in use, and the knowledge they’ve encoded becomes something the organization owns.

It has been revealed that many planning teams will choose next year’s tools in the coming weeks, and vendor demos won’t make that choice easier. Planners are a skeptical lot by nature, and some vendor claims deserve extra skepticism.

The clearest test is whether a tool can model your process, not the vendor’s. AI-native systems are composable by nature – they offer as much flexibility as a spreadsheet, with the power of an enterprise planning platform.

Sources indicate that here’s how to test it. Bring one workflow your team runs today, with its real quirks: how you allocate scarce inventory across customers, which suppliers get extra buffer, when a planner overrides the forecast. Ask the vendor to set it up on your data and walk through it. An AI-native platform can flex to fit how your team works and let you add steps as the process changes. If the answer is that your team will need to adapt to the system’s standard workflow, you are looking at a legacy platform with a chat window on top.

Industry observers note that michael Rossiter is co-founder and CEO of Atomic, an AI-native supply planning platform. He previously spent several years in Tesla’s supply chain organization, where he served as Director of Sales Operations and helped build the planning system that took Tesla through the Model 3 ramp. He is also a partner at DVx Ventures.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • It has been revealed that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

It has been revealed that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

It has been revealed that for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

According to recent reports, GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Sources indicate that serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Recent findings suggest that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

Industry News: Security incident on Hex.pm

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hex

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers.
  • We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems.
  • According to recent reports, because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

According to recent reports, because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm. Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm.

We checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

The attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a newly introduced registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514.

hex.pm decoded unauthenticated request bodies in Erlang term format with Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 which blocks most potentially harmful terms, but allows struct values through. These decoded struct values, when chained together correctly, turned into a remote command execution (RCE). This is the detailed playbook of the attack:.

While investigating, we found the same class of vulnerability in Ash: its keyset pagination accepted crafted structs in client-supplied cursors, which could lead to command execution or SQL injection. We reported it and the Ash team released a fix in ash 3.38.0 on November 24. It is tracked as CVE-2026-124283.

hexpm commit 379b0a2 makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, returning a 400. Because the check sits in the one decoder used for this format, it covers every route that accepts it. That closes the entry point: an attacker can no longer get a fake struct into the request params. Every hex.pm server was running the patched build by 18:31 UTC.

We are working on hardening fixes for these libraries which should prevent such an attack in the future on multiple levels, not just one decoder check in the request pipeline:.

Recent findings suggest that every finding in this post is based on the checks below. Where a check is still running or something can't be verified from our logs, we say so.

We're sorry for the inconvenience these precautions cause. If you have questions or notice anything unusual in your account, contact us at support@hex.pm. Security reports can be sent to security@hex.pm. We'll update this post as our investigation continues.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • John Harrington is Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of HighByte, where he leads business and product strategy, including product management and customer and partner success.
  • HighByte is an industrial software firm focused on the data architecture and integration challenges manufacturers face.
  • In a recent development, before co-founding HighByte in 2018, you held leadership roles at Kepware and PTC, and had worked alongside your fellow founders since 2012.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

John Harrington is Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of HighByte, where he leads business and product strategy, including product management and customer and partner success. His career spans manufacturing operations and industrial software, giving him experience with both the challenges of using plant-floor data and the technology needed to connect it across an enterprise.

HighByte is an industrial software firm focused on the data architecture and integration challenges manufacturers face. Its Intelligence Hub provides an Industrial DataOps layer for connecting, modeling, contextualizing, and delivering operational data to enterprise applications, cloud platforms, and AI systems.

In a recent development, before co-founding HighByte in 2018, you held leadership roles at Kepware and PTC, and had worked alongside your fellow founders since 2012. What specific interoperability or security problem convinced you that manufacturers needed an entirely new industrial data platform, and how has that original vision evolved with the rise of AI?

I’ve worked in manufacturing and industrial environments for nearly my entire career. In these roles, I’ve had the opportunity to view industrial data from both sides of the coin, working at a manufacturer that made data-driven decisions and a number of software providers that enable digitalization and smart manufacturing.

In a recent development, this is a significant challenge. For one thing, users often need data that is curated differently than how most execution systems—MES solutions, ERPs, data historians, or otherwise—choose to store it. If they are lucky, they might be able to copy data from these systems and paste it into Excel to be analyzed and compared. Unfortunately, this method takes a lot of time, delays their decision-making, and requires access to domain experts who can explain the nuances of the data being reviewed.

Industry observers note that luckily, today’s data storage and analysis systems are tremendous. Cloud platforms like AWS and Azure and data warehouse providers like Snowflake and Databricks have simplified the scale challenge, creating unified repositories for industrial data across plants and offering easy access for business consumers through applications and LLMs. Still, there’s a larger need to link these capable operational systems with emerging cloud and AI solutions, which itself requires the automated delivery of usable, contextualized, and compliant data.

Like any other business, AI has had an impact on the way HighByte operates. On the one hand, we’ve incorporated AI into our platform, creating a Pipeline AI Agent and a Modeling Agent for LLM-assisted pipeline, model, and instance generation and management. But these solutions have also changed how customers use and interact with industrial data in their day-to-day operations. By establishing a foundation of connected, contextualized, high-quality data for our customers, we provide the critical information that LLMs and agents need to operate effectively and efficiently in manufacturing environments.

Manufacturers are often eager to deploy AI before addressing the condition of their underlying data. What does a robust Industrial DataOps strategy look like in practice, and what warning signs indicate that a company’s data foundation is not ready for AI?

Industry observers note that it’s key to note that any Industrial DataOps strategy should be part of an organization’s more comprehensive Industrial Data Strategy, which encompasses a broad view of organizational scope, applications, data platforms, integrations, networks, governance, and regulatory requirements. Within this larger strategy, a more targeted Industrial DataOps approach can address integration requirements and focus on delivering usable data to required applications based on established contracts and cadences. This involves creating a robust data foundation and defining standard data products and pipelines for each application or use case.

Sources indicate that any company that lacks a strong data foundation will not be capable of successful AI deployment at scale. It’s as simple as that. An effective Industrial DataOps strategy is one that ensures data is contextualized, connected, governed, and trusted before it’s consumed by applications or AI models.

Manufacturers should be careful not to rush AI deployments if their data is not yet up to the task. The warning signs are easy to spot: siloed systems, inconsistent naming conventions, duplicate data pipelines, and teams spending more time and effort finding data than actually using it. If you’re still debating which version of your data is accurate, you’re not ready to implement and scale AI solutions.

It has been revealed that AI agents work best when they have very focused objectives and a limited number of capable tools at their disposal to access data. Overly broad agents with too many potential tools and unclear data resources will inevitably result in hallucinations and incorrect decisions, ultimately doing more harm than good.

In a recent development, industrial data is frequently fragmented across programmable logic controllers, manufacturing execution systems, historians, enterprise applications, and cloud platforms. What context must be added to this raw data before an AI model or agent can reliably interpret it and make useful decisions?

In a recent development, imagine if I dropped you in the middle of a supermarket and asked you to buy me the items that I need. No detail, no list, no direction. Even worse, the aisle markers and signage are nowhere to be found. What do you think the odds are that you’d get me exactly what I’m looking for?

This is the type of scenario that AI models and agents are likely to find themselves in without proper context. Even with access to raw manufacturing data, this information alone cannot provide sufficient guidance for AI models to take accurate and impactful action. They need as much context as possible in order to effectively carry out their assigned tasks and provide reliable output.

It has been revealed that going back to the supermarket example, imagine if I asked you to specifically buy the supplies I need to create a PB&J sandwich. You could walk into the store, find the proper aisles based on the clearly marked signage, and get me the bread, peanut butter, jelly, and a knife for spreading. Maybe even some potato chips on the side.

In the same way, a predictive maintenance agent in an Industrial DataOps system can rely on clearly contextualized data to meet its needs. The agent can cite clearly marked temperature, pressure, and vibration data and compare it against historical performance, allowing it to recognize any relevant fluctuations and take preventative action as needed.

You have predicted that agentic AI could produce a hundredfold increase in edge-based data consumers, with specialized agents supporting maintenance, quality, scheduling, and supply chain operations. How must traditional factory data architecture change to support this scale without creating thousands of brittle integrations?

Sources indicate that traditional industrial data architectures were designed to support a handful of applications consuming data in each factory. Now, agentic AI is set to completely change that equation. Instead of managing dozens of data consumers, manufacturers will need to support thousands of automated, specialized agents moving forward.

The answer here isn’t thousands of fresh point-to-point integrations. Instead, it’s a centralized data layer that can contextualize, govern, and securely deliver the right data product to the right consumer at the right time—regardless of whether it’s a human user or an automated agent. Accessibility, context, and governance will all be key for maximizing the full potential of AI solutions on the factory floor.

In a recent development, highByte has introduced Model Context Protocol services that allow industrial data pipelines to be exposed as tools for AI agents. How does Model Context Protocol complement existing standards such as Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport, and application programming interfaces, and what governance is required to prevent agents from accessing the wrong tools or data?

In a recent development, OPC UA and MQTT were designed for reading and writing device-level data, while APIs were designed for interacting directly with applications. MCP was designed specifically for interacting with LLMs. The HighByte Intelligence Hub is a middleware layer that unites these protocols, interacting with each device, system, and agent using their preferred protocol and curating data products using data from one or more sources.

Just as importantly, Intelligence Hub creates a layer of control and governance between agents and operational systems. Rather than giving agents unrestricted access to data, manufacturers can govern what tools the agents can access, which systems they can interact with, and what kinds of decisions they can influence.

Traditionally, governance was applied in the application layer through user-role-based access controls. As manufacturers deploy more agents across maintenance, quality, scheduling, and supply chain operations, traditional applications go away and agent-specific governance becomes crucial. In an agentic ecosystem, the governance of data flows effectively becomes the mechanism for governing the overall actions of AI agents.

In a recent development, the Pipeline AI Agent in HighByte Intelligence Hub allows users to create, explain, and modify industrial data pipelines through natural language while retaining human review. Which DataOps responsibilities are well suited to AI automation, and where should human approval remain mandatory?

In a recent development, deploying complex data pipelines is often iterative and, as a result, relatively challenging. With the HighByte Intelligence Hub, we have provided multiple modes for easily creating, modifying, and managing both modeling and pipeline configuration tasks. A user can manually create and modify their own configurations, leverage the Pipeline and Modeling Agents for AI-driven assistance, and use MCP configuration tools to fully configure the Intelligence Hub externally with an agent. We expect that the user will select the most appropriate method based on their experience level with the Intelligence Hub and AI and the size and scope of the changes.

It has been revealed that given all these methods of configuration, the system will need to be tested and validated. This is done in real time by agents that observe and approve any changes being applied. The agents are also great at explaining what the configuration does for troubleshooting and documentation purposes.

Sources indicate that global manufacturers need common data standards across facilities, but every plant has different equipment, processes, and operational requirements. How can companies create reusable industrial data products while preserving the local context that makes the data meaningful?

It has been revealed that this is one of the core benefits of a robust Industrial DataOps strategy and platform. When different facilities are unified under a single platform, teams can align and standardize data collection and naming practices across different sites, while still maintaining the flexibility needed to account for site-specific context.

Sources indicate that the key is to separate standardization from uniformity. Manufacturers should establish common enterprise models, naming conventions, and governance policies, but at the same time should still allow sites to capture the operational context unique to each facility’s processes and outputs. For example, a bottling line in one facility may operate differently than an equivalent line elsewhere, but both can still map to a shared enterprise data model.

Industry observers note that highByte recently partnered with Siemens to combine industrial edge connectivity, contextualized data, and tools for building AI models and agents. Does this type of collaboration signal that the future industrial AI stack will be built through interoperable ecosystems rather than a single end-to-end platform?

Yes, the future industrial AI stack won’t be owned by any one firm; it will be built on interoperable technologies that each solve a specific problem well. HighByte partnered with Siemens because we both recognized that successful industrial AI requires both operational connectivity and trusted, contextualized data. Together, Siemens Industrial Edge and HighByte Intelligence Hub help manufacturers bridge the gap between IT and OT systems; connecting data from machinery, SCADA, historians, MES, ERP and all the rest of the systems in and around the factory into a unified data infrastructure that AI can actually use.

In a recent development, AI agents are only as effective as the data they consume, and each operational system provides a piece of the puzzle for the agent, but not the entire puzzle. Open, interoperable ecosystems give manufacturers the flexibility to innovate with best-in-breed solutions without creating fresh silos or vendor lock-in. By combining Siemens’ industrial connectivity capacity with HighByte’s DataOps capabilities, manufacturers can more easily connect, contextualize, and consume industrial data to scale AI models and agents across the enterprise.

Recent findings suggest that predictive maintenance, quality inspection, energy optimization, and production planning are all frequently presented as promising industrial AI applications. How should manufacturers select their first use case, establish measurable business value, and avoid becoming trapped in a cycle of pilots that never scale?

It has been revealed that it’s essential that manufacturers start with a problem they need to solve, not a technology they want to adopt. The best first use case is one that is causing frustration today, has actual measurable business value, ties to accessible data, and has a clear path to operational adoption. Once that has been achieved, you can take your learnings and apply AI to tackle the next challenge.

In a recent development, today, too many teams are focusing on deploying isolated pilots, when they should really be prioritizing the underlying data architecture that’s required to scale AI across systems, sites, and enterprise infrastructure. Success will come not from a single use case, but instead, from building a reusable foundation that supports multiple AI deployments over time and expands in tandem with increasing AI integration.

Looking ahead, how do you expect AI agents to change the roles of plant operators, engineers, and data teams, and what technical or organizational barrier must be solved before manufacturers can safely give these systems greater autonomy?

I don’t foresee a world where AI agents fully replace manufacturing professionals, but I do see one where AI changes how they work. With the support of effective agents, operators will be able to spend less time searching for information and more time making impactful, informed decisions. Engineers will be tasked with overseeing and optimizing fleets of highly specialized agents, and data teams will shift from report building to data product and AI system governance.

Recent findings suggest that the real differentiator in this AI-driven future will be how effectively manufacturers can deploy and govern specialized agents that can take autonomous action on trusted industrial data for real business challenges. Those who solve the data and governance challenge early will be the ones who realize the greatest value from AI. The ultimate value of AI for manufacturers is to reduce downtime, increase throughput, reduce defects and scrap, improve safety, reduce costs, and improve the agility of the business to react to supply and demand changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something latest, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

It has been revealed that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

It has been revealed that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

According to recent reports, boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Industry observers note that for edits, each region indicates where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

It has been revealed that everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

Sources indicate that A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

Sources indicate that so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

Recent findings suggest that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Sources indicate that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

Recent findings suggest that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

It has been revealed that at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

Recent findings suggest that in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

In a recent development, text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Sources indicate that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps highlights how the image takes shape:.

It has been revealed that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TIDAL will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog on December 9, 2026, Robert Andersen confirmed on November 24, 2026. He said the plan would delete 29 million songs and leave the catalog clear of those tracks by the beginning of 2027.

Andersen’s X profile claims he runs TIDAL at Block, while Block’s leadership page identifies him as the company’s principal designer. TIDAL’s official account confirmed the start date on X, writing, “Bye AI music. Starting December 9.”.

Recent findings suggest that andersen mentioned TIDAL tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks a few months earlier to protect real artists’ authenticity, but that 43% of tracks distributed to the service in the preceding 90 days had been detected as AI-generated and 96% of AI-generated songs received zero plays. Those figures describe a large detected inflow with little listening for AI-generated material. The new policy adds deletion to the earlier labeling and demonetization approach.

Recent findings suggest that andersen estimated that TIDAL would reject 80,000 to 85,000 AI-generated songs per day, described the manufacturer as the first digital service provider to take this step, and encouraged competing services to follow. The daily figure covers expected future rejections, distinct from deletions of music already in the catalog.

TIDAL’s terms, effective June 29, 2026, for the service outside Canada, the European Union, the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom, define AI-generated content as audio wholly or substantially generated by generative AI with limited or no direct human creative input beyond an initial text prompt or similar instruction. The revealed removal applies to wholly AI-generated tracks, a narrower formulation than that contractual definition.

Those terms provide for an in-app AI indicator at track or album level. Identification and labeling are performed on a best-efforts basis using industry-standard detection technology; TIDAL cautions that detection can produce false positives and false negatives and does not warrant the accuracy or completeness of a label or its absence.

In a recent development, under the same terms, TIDAL Upload tracks may be scanned for AI generation, AI-generated uploads are ineligible for monetization, and people who believe a track was erroneously tagged can contact support. The rules already give classification direct financial consequences for uploaders.

TIDAL’s published content guidelines say the service accepts AI-generated content that meets additional requirements. For AI-generated content, they prohibit material that impersonates or imitates an artist’s voice, likeness or identity without express authorization, misleads listeners about its origin or creation, or perpetuates streaming fraud, including inflated play counts and royalties diverted from legitimate artists.

It has been revealed that violations may be labeled, demonetized or removed without prior notice, while repeated or egregious breaches can bring account suspension or termination. Moderation combines automated scanning at upload with human review when necessary. Consumers can appeal content removals and account decisions, with human moderators reassessing the material and initial decision; account suspensions and terminations also receive human review before being finalized.

The announcement moves TIDAL beyond disclosure and demonetization toward using AI detection to determine catalog access. Since the published terms acknowledge mistaken classifications, the policy’s practical impact will depend on how reliably TIDAL distinguishes wholly generated music from human-directed work and how effectively its review process handles disputes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.

Industry observers note that yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.

According to recent reports, every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.

Industry observers note that he illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

On failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need significant-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.

According to recent reports, for team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.

Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers right now do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

In a recent development, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

It has been revealed that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that intends, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Sources indicate that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

According to recent reports, grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Industry observers note that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

Recent findings suggest that the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

It has been revealed that the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:.

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:.

Sources indicate that the repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

In a recent development, llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

It has been revealed that the checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:.

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:.

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

Industry observers note that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

According to recent reports, note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

In a recent development, this is a massive model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/fresh/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section reveals how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In a recent development, in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Industry observers note that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

It has been revealed that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

Sources indicate that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

Sources indicate that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Industry observers note that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Sources indicate that you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Industry observers note that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#92375. The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1543 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track.
  • Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.
  • Security researcher Patrick Wardle showed that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track. Four questions to help executives get ahead of it.

Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.

The signal arrived in September. Security researcher Patrick Wardle showed that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices. Muse works across files, email, messages and calendar, so whoever controls the session inherits all of it. Meta shipped a fix within a day.

The flaw matters less than what it exposes. Most conversations about personal agents ask whether the agent is safe for the person using it. At work, the question changes. When an employee connects a personal agent to organization email or Slack, it becomes an autonomous actor inside company systems that security never approved. It has an insider’s access and an insider’s credentials, and none of the controls companies apply to insiders: no background check, no security training, no offboarding. Companies built employee security around people, and the agent acting for each person gets no attention. I expect incidents like this to become routine in 2027.

Four questions separate the security teams in control from the ones guessing.

Which personal agents are already connected to work accounts?

Recent findings suggest that start here, because everything else depends on the answer. Shadow AI can account for more than 60% of an enterprise’s AI assets, and personal agents add to that share.

In one deployment, a single employee machine had about 400 agent skills installed, and roughly half of them were malicious. The employee had not chosen them. They came bundled with an AI app installed for work. Public marketplaces show the same pattern: roughly 12% of the skills in one audit were malicious.

Recent findings suggest that many of these agents run on the desktop, where browser-based monitoring cannot see them. I see the same pattern in customer environments. A organization blocks ChatGPT in the browser, so employees download the desktop app or use a personal account. I consider this the most underhyped blind spot in enterprise AI.

Industry observers note that blocking has also stopped being the default answer. A year ago, roughly nine out of ten of my customer conversations began with “we do not approve AI in our organization.” Today the question is how to enable employees safely, and that starts with an inventory. The cost of skipping it is documented: 92% of organizations with an AI-related breach lacked proper AI access controls.

Sources indicate that if I had 90 days and one project, I would spend them here. Complete visibility across employee machines, desktops included, is a significant win on its own. In 2027, I expect personal agents to become as ordinary as the browser, so security has to follow the agent down to the individual employee: which agents each person runs, what those agents connect to and what they did.

Are approval and spending limits enforced outside the model?

It has been revealed that “Ask me before you spend” is a request typed into the agent. It holds for as long as the agent honors it, and instructions can be forgotten, argued around or overwritten by an attacker.

Industry observers note that the stronger design puts the limit outside the model. Even Meta designed Muse so that a separate component, outside the sandbox where the model runs, approves each request, and executives should expect the same arrangement for employee agents.

Tier the limits by risk. Low-risk, reversible actions such as reading a calendar can run automatically. Drafting a reply can run inside defined limits. Moving money, deleting data, sharing files externally and anything irreversible should wait for a person.

In a recent development, requiring approval for everything creates fatigue and removes the value of the agent. A policy written into the task prompt also falls short. Runtime controls, enforced where the agent cannot edit them, have moved from nice to have to must-have. The industry calls the underlying risk excessive agency: more functionality, permission and autonomy than the task requires. As agents start booking, buying and paying in 2027, I expect transaction authorization to become a major concern. Approval will need to be tied to the specific payee and amount, not to a broad permission to spend granted months earlier.

There is a catch, and Muse indicates it too. Meta had this design in place, and the hijack still worked, because the attacker did not need to argue with the agent. It held the agent’s session. Limits outside the model govern what the agent may do. They cannot tell the agent apart from someone holding its keys. That is the job of identity.

Does every agent have its own identity?

If an agent signs in as the employee, every action looks like the employee took it. Investigators cannot tell whether the person or the agent sent a message, and the manufacturer cannot switch off the agent without switching off the person. Shared credentials are one of the biggest violations I see.

Personal agents complicate this, because a company cannot concern an identity to an agent an employee bought on a personal account. It does control the connection point. Access to company email and Slack runs through grants the company can see and govern, so it can require agents to connect through approved apps with their own scoped tokens, refuse connections that reuse the employee’s login and revoke any single grant without touching the employee’s account.

In a recent development, A separate identity also answers the departure question. Companies have become reasonably good at cutting off access when an employee leaves, but only the access they know exists. An agent with its own identity can be revoked that day.

Scope matters as much, and the Muse flaw indicates why: one captured token carried everything the assistant was allowed to do. Read access to one Slack channel limits what a stolen token can do. Access to the whole workspace “just in case” sets the limit at everything.

Moving a credential into a secrets manager improves how it is stored and leaves its scope unchanged. Few teams revisit scope after the pilot, when a token minted for a two-week test quietly becomes the permission the agent runs on indefinitely.

Do you know what normal looks like?

In a recent development, visibility, limits and identity reduce exposure, and they will not catch everything. Teams also need a baseline of how each agent normally behaves: which tools it uses, what data it touches and the order in which it acts. The baseline has to come from the organization’s own traffic, because normal for one organization’s agents looks nothing like normal for another’s.

Agent activity differs from human activity in ways a baseline can capture. A person pauses, second-guesses and goes deep on a few leads. An agent moves from reconnaissance to action almost immediately, keeps the same pace at step three and step three hundred, and probes many systems at once.

Defenders hold an advantage here, because context is the one thing an attacking agent cannot shortcut. An attacker’s agent does not know which systems normally talk to each other or which data a given team touches, so it has to probe, and probing looks different from work. You do not need to catch the attack that works. You need to notice the looking.

According to recent reports, respond in steps. Watch the agent, flag it, slow it down, and block only when confident, with unclear cases going to a person. Trust in automated response also depends on explainability. If an analyst cannot see in plain language why an agent was flagged, they will never let automation act alone.

Industry observers note that personal agents will keep arriving, and employees will keep connecting them to the tools they use all day. The leaders who stay in control will find the agents first, enforce limits outside the model, give each agent an identity and learn what normal looks like.

Visibility comes first, and everything else follows from it.

Sources indicate that how many personal agents are connected to your company’s email and Slack today? If the honest answer is a guess, that is where the first 90 days belong.

In a recent development, ankita Gupta is the Co-founder and CEO of Akto, an enterprise Agentic AI Security and Governance platform helping organizations discover, monitor, and secure AI agents across their environments. She brings 15+ years of experience across cybersecurity, engineering, and enterprise technology, having held roles at JPMorgan, LinkedIn, and VMware. She works with Fortune 1000 enterprises to address emerging security challenges associated with AI adoption, autonomous agents, and the evolving AI threat landscape.
